panels.body_site: neck (retropharyngeal space and right internal jugular vein)
panels.rationale: Contrast-enhanced axial CT of the neck in a Lemierre syndrome case series, showing right internal jugular vein enlargement with intraluminal thrombus (septic thrombophlebitis) and adjacent retropharyngeal soft-tissue infection/abscess; the caption and article title directly attribute these manifestations to Lemierre syndrome. Yellow arrow annotation is present. Single-panel figure.
panels.attribution_text: Alyousef et al. Expanding the clinical spectrum of Lemierre syndrome and Lemierre-like septic internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis: a four-case series. Frontiers in medicine None. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrating retropharyngeal soft-tissue swelling and fluid collection consistent with soft-tissue infection/abscess formation. There is enlargement of the right internal jugular vein extending to the right brachiocephalic vein with a large intraluminal thrombus measuring more than 8 cm in length.
in_text_mentions: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the neck demonstrated retropharyngeal soft-tissue infection with phlegmon formation and an abscess extending from C1 to C5–C6, causing mild airway narrowing without obstruction. CT also revealed enlargement and thrombosis of the right internal jugular vein, accompanied by marked perivascular inflammatory changes, consistent with septic thrombophlebitis (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single contrast-enhanced axial neck CT panel from a Lemierre syndrome case series. The caption and in-text description explicitly identify right internal jugular vein thrombosis with extension, matching the Lemierre syndrome vocabulary finding. The circled right carotid space multiloculated abscess is also described, but no exact vocabulary key exists for it, so it is recorded as a proposed finding.

in_text_mentions: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a multiloculated abscess with irregular peripheral enhancement within the right carotid space. The palatine tonsils were enlarged, more pronounced on the right, with small areas of low attenuation. Imaging also revealed thrombosis of the right internal jugular vein with associated wall enhancement (Figure 7). The thrombus extended intracranially into the right sigmoid and transverse venous sinuses and inferiorly to the level of C7.

in_text_mentions: Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed multiple bilateral nodules, most of which were cavitated (Figure 1A, B). Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck revealed a hypoechoic thrombus filling the right internal jugular vein (Figure 1C, D). Color Doppler imaging revealed a thrombus and the absence of detectable intraluminal flow (Figure 1E). The patient was diagnosed with Lemierre syndrome secondary to oropharyngeal infection. Her symptoms improved with antibioticotherapy, and she was discharged in a stable condition.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Longitudinal B-mode ultrasound of the left neck demonstrating an echogenic thrombus filling the internal jugular vein lumen in a patient with Lemierre syndrome; panel-specific caption and in-text description support the diagnosis. B: Color Doppler ultrasound of the left internal jugular vein showing an intraluminal thrombus with no detectable flow, the characteristic vascular manifestation of Lemierre syndrome. C: Ultrasound panel labeled 'abscess' showing the 3.9 x 2.6 cm left anterolateral neck abscess posterolateral to the sternocleidomastoid muscle described in the caption; the finding is not in the provided vocabulary so it is listed as a proposed finding. It is part of the same patient's Lemierre syndrome presentation.

Additionally, a heterogeneous hypoechoic collection measuring 3.9 cm by 2.6 cm was identified in the left anterolateral neck, located posterolateral to the left sternocleidomastoid muscle. These findings led to a diagnosis of acute thrombosis of the left IJV and an anterolateral neck abscess.
